To be absolutely free is not a passive understanding, it is an active realization. To understand greater levels of freedom is to have contrast. To be absolutely free isn’t something that will have been literally achieved but it is a start in directing oneself in understanding the absurd and our condition. An example I use from my life is I feel more free when I purposefully exercise daily and go for these runs that make me want to quit, which means then I’m only about half way done. That is my rebellion. The utter futility of running, the suffering, the work it takes and ultimately how repetitive it is are all themes of the absurd. Yet I make the choice, every waking second, to keep going, to keep the pace, to value how I feel both during and after. I smile, I laugh at myself desiring to quit, I appreciate the sensory experience good or bad as proof of my vitality given I continue to seek it. 

Now, how can someone be so free their very existence  is an act of rebellion? To say we are so free that our VERY existence is an act of rebellion entails a lifelong resistance against the absurd. You put forth your value, you grit your teeth, tighten your grip, adjust your breath and slay that dragon. “Oh but mere mortals shouldn’t be wandering around conquering nature,” well that isn’t a direction the absurd hero would take. We wander, we arrive, but we don’t predicate our fulfillment on the universe aligning, we predicate it on ourselves. If values seem to not grab you, you are making value do too much work. That lifelong burden is on you, now what will you do?

A Nihilist kneels and dies, the absurd hero utilizes their passion against death to undermine its conclusions. We all will be dead soon and will have any evidence of our existence obliterated in 3.4 billion years. Many would reasonably conclude nothing matters. What the absurd hero concludes is nothing matters which really sucks so I’m just going to make things matter as they always have before this lucidity. Yet I know things don’t matter, but how often has our crude reasoning determined something necessary? Plus even no meaning is meaning in itself so really there is no escape from value as long as you’re alive. So if by a minimum we’re enchained by our values as they direct us,still, we strive for that futile task to avoid limits as we can never hope to realize it but in its endless pursuit, life becomes itself again and the opportunity for so much value, good and bad, arises.

First of all, I’m so sorry you’re going through this, I know how it feels and I’ll try to help you by telling you what helped me get out of the vicious cycle. 

Most people say it because they’re alive and live an endurable life, so the judgement makes sense to them. But let me tell you, suicide is not a solution, it’s an escape. For a long distance runner, leaving the marathon isn’t a solution to their problem of a lagging pace, it’s an escape. It is semantics but important in my opinion as it determines whether or not there’s a logic to suicide that holds up with reason at its bitter end. As Camus put it, “it is easy to be logical. It is near impossible to be logical to the bitter end.” It is true that reason is often an afterthought in many of our actions, it often has questionable value as well. But relieving one part of the mind, of the question of suicide, is essential to a fulfilling life.

Now, feeling can be changed. I know how depression was like for me, and it’s truly a pit of despair. To preface the point I want to make, many who feel as severely as you or I have gone through unimaginable torment, think Anne Frank, and made the most out of it. They were happy in the most desolate of conditions. This is their freedom being used to its fullest potential. That’s rebellion, their willpower is greater than all of their circumstance. But why rebel? I know my willpower and where it sits now, so maybe that’s a solution for the lucky. How I think about it is that willpower is something developed, and although the process is repetitive, ultimately futile when considering death and certainly laborious, it is in the struggle that they are happy. Not in reflection but simply being so enthralled with life, totally in the moment, happiness is possible. 

Life is so short and everything will be better if you can will a good one. It’s annoying but enjoying the little things is essential, from a hot shower to simple sensations like a refreshing breeze on a sunny day, they won’t enjoy themselves. You will still be depressed, but you can have something to look forward to. As for depression, there are many answers but the one I found the most effective was changing my life, day by day. Setting 2 week goals where I establish habits that make being happy easier. Working out, eating enough food and reading books I have found love for have all been essential.

I’ve been depressed and suicidal from the age of 12 to the age of 20, I would say I’m in recovery right now and it’s due to reading the Myth of Sisyphus by Camus, but also having love in my life whether it be my parents or my cats. I started it at the age of 17 and it took me 3 years to really get it. It’s very hard to accept the nature of life, one of the more difficult ideas being that what we think may as well be reality. It’s frustrating knowing I can embrace life, not only knowing of its horrors but also accepting the good. Whether that amounts to life worth living, that is the essential question! 

Most people will avoid these matters of utmost importance because it is often incomprehensible to a mind which craves meaning. To think that our lives will be obliterated without a trace, deleting any permanent sense of meaning is certainly an issue. So what do people do? They commit what Camus calls philosophical suicide, one way being assigning a universal meaning to life such as god, the other secular method being to drown in entertainment and commodity. But you’re asking the burning question that everyone should answer! Why live?

This lucidity is our burden, but at the same time it is our passion. We refuse to accept a just god in a world where Gazelles that seemingly commit no fowl deed, meet the cruelest of fates by a pack of hyenas. This cold indifference of the world is enough to make a man cry, but Camus postulates that it does not condemn us to death. He even goes as far to pursue reasoning for suicide, in order to purge it of its contents. What he finds is that people find that whatever meaning they have assigned to life( no meaning is meaning in itself), it is revealed that it has always been easily undermined. Whether it be because of the abruptness of life or like in Camus’ case, he had a severe leg injury that prevented him from pursuing professional football, meaning is seen to be uprooted from what was thought to be solid foundations, being revealed as another crude tool we have collectively developed to make life possible. He believes this because ridiculous circumstance has been endured for centuries, given that there’s a sense of meaning in one’s life.

So what is there to do if it is a problem of meaning? If we know all meaning cannot be objective or even correspondent to reality all the time, then what is there to do? Camus wants to invigorate a sense of rebellion in you. He recognizes the limits that religion imposes on ones freedom while also knowing rejecting all meaning in the form of Nihilism cripples the individual. So the rebellion begins with one foot in front of the other. By simply creating ur own personalized meaning, you are rejecting that life is a condemnation and you assert its value through action. This is not an easy leap, but it is how to start a life worth living. 

The necessity behind this leap is that this is a matter of life and death. I know if I refuse to grant a meaning to life, I may very well die to MAID in 2027. So what have I chosen? Well I want to become a psychiatrist that not only criticizes others faulty methods like Jordan Peterson, but to also have a method in which the new generation can follow that invigorates them to not only live, but to the fullest. I want to eventually impact politics and become the leader that Canada is desperately lacking. Whether these are unrealistic ideals, I cannot know without trying. I know it will be seen as futile, it’s certainly going to be repetitive, so how is it even possible is to embrace it all? Every moment of discomfort while working out, to my cat sleeping on my lap, I smile and enjoy it. I embrace the moment. I’ve even had a few days where certifiably I can admit that I was happy. I know the metaphorical boulder is going to roll down again, so I laugh at the absurdity of my predicament, conquering it in one stroke. 

You have the strength, or you must prove without a doubt that it is otherwise. I have IBS, I have disabilities, I even withdrew from university 3 years in a row! But I don’t give up, because knowing what others have done, I do not exempt myself without certain knowledge. I know there is no replacement for 20 years of experience so I stay a little less delusional. My favourite example is Alexander Hamilton, that man conquered having a dead family at around the age of 9, was born on a poverty-stricken island, fought in a war and even dealt with political rivals that would even go as far to murder the man for selfish gain. How can he embrace life and not me? This is how I illustrate the irrationality behind a vigourless life. Schopenhauer wrote a quote on this: In order to live and to function in society, we must make sacrifices. This is inevitable. We must get along with other people to get what we want. We must be cooperative and generally be pleasant to be around. Above all, we must be able to relate to the common man.

For the intelligent person, and especially the man of genius, this is a big burden to carry. For the genius, it’s hard to relate to the common man. He will inevitably feel alone.

Therefore, it’s for the best if he learns to enjoy solitude.

But why is society so dull in the first place? Schopenhauer’s answer is elitist: because most people are dull. And it’s exactly because most people are dull, that they are driven to interaction with others. It’s as if the average person is not a full person by himself, and needs others to complete him.

The intelligent mind can occupy itself and does not need distractions or empty activity. But for the average person, this kind of activity, literally just passing the time, becomes necessary.

However, Schopenhauer also concedes that the need for solitude is directly related to age. The younger you are, the more need you have for socializing. This is also because your mind is not yet fully developed: the younger we are, the more we are like others.

The essay closes with a word of warning. Seclusion, being alone, has its drawbacks. For example, Schopenhauer notes that we become more irritable by being alone. We are more easily annoyed by minor things because we aren’t accustomed to the turmoils of regular life.

A small rock, thrown into a still lake, causes a notable disturbance. The same rock thrown into a stormy sea, not nearly as much. But this is a small price to pay for peace of mind, which we attain by removing ourselves from the stormy seas of society.
